editorial_assessment: All five openings stay within egg-case parasitism and the documented lack of stinging or biting. None diagnoses an active infestation or promises whole-home control.

hooks.text: An ensign wasp in your house can look like a reason to worry about stings. But this wasp doesn’t sting or bite people. Its young feed on cockroach eggs.
hooks.payoff: Explain the difference between the harmless adult wasp a homeowner sees and its developing larva feeding inside a cockroach egg case.

hooks.text: A female ensign wasp adds just one egg to a cockroach’s egg case. When that egg hatches, the roach eggs become food.
hooks.payoff: Follow the single wasp egg into the larval stage and explain how that larva feeds on multiple cockroach eggs.

hooks.text: A cockroach egg case can hold more than developing roaches. Inside, an ensign wasp larva may be growing by eating the eggs around it.
hooks.payoff: Reveal what can happen inside a cockroach egg case after a female ensign wasp deposits an egg there.

hooks.text: How does an ensign wasp attack cockroaches before they even hatch? It starts by laying an egg inside their egg case.
hooks.payoff: Explain how the wasp’s offspring feeds on cockroach eggs, targeting the egg stage of the host species.

hooks.text: Picture a mother wasp leaving her egg surrounded by food for her young. For an ensign wasp, that nursery is a cockroach egg case—and the food is cockroach eggs.
hooks.payoff: Explain how placing an egg inside a cockroach egg case puts the developing wasp larva together with its food.
